summary.text: An induction on bipartization distance gives bounds $N(d)$ such that every finite non-three-colorable graph contains, for some $d>0$, an induced subgraph on at most $N(d)$ vertices requiring at least $d$ edge deletions; it uses bounded short odd-walk obstructions or compresses a plateau between nested balls with a two-apex boundary closure. Choosing a divergent $f$ diagonally so that $f(N(d))<d$ forces every finite induced subgraph, and hence by coloring compactness the whole graph, to be three-colorable.

full_proof.text:
We disprove the stated assertion by constructing one function \(f:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N\), tending to infinity, for which every graph satisfying the required local bound is in fact 3-colorable. Such a graph cannot have infinite chromatic number.

Throughout the proof, all graphs appearing in finite constructions are finite. If \(H\) is a finite graph, write
\[
 \beta(H)
\]
for the minimum number of edges which must be deleted from \(H\) to make it bipartite. Equivalently,
\[
 \beta(H)=\min_{c:V(H)\to\{0,1\}}
 \bigl|\{xy\in E(H):c(x)=c(y)\}\bigr|. \tag{1}
\]
Indeed, for any binary coloring \(c\), deleting all monochromatic edges leaves a properly 2-colored graph. Conversely, if deleting a set \(F\) leaves a bipartite graph, a proper binary coloring of \(H-F\) can have monochromatic edges only in \(F\). Thus the two minima agree.

For a graph \(H\) and a vertex set \(X\), let \(H[X]\) denote the graph containing exactly the edges of \(H\) whose two endpoints lie in \(X\); retaining vertices outside \(X\) as isolated vertices makes no difference to \(\beta\). We use the following elementary consequences of (1).

1. If \(H_1\) is a subgraph of \(H_2\) on the same finite vertex set, then
\[
 \beta(H_1)\leq \beta(H_2).
\]
More generally, an injective graph homomorphism from \(H_1\) into \(H_2\) implies \(\beta(H_1)\leq\beta(H_2)\): pull an optimal binary coloring of \(H_2\) back to \(H_1\).

2. For a finite set \(X\subseteq V(G)\),
\[
 \beta(G[X])\leq
 G.\operatorname{maxSubgraphEdgeDistToBipartite}(|X|). \tag{2}
\]
This follows by taking the subgraph of \(G\) induced on \(X\) in the definition of the maximum.

3. \(\beta(H)=0\) if and only if \(H\) is bipartite.

The heart of the argument is a uniform finite-witness theorem. We first develop the ingredients needed for it.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
1. A bounded-radius kernel
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Define numbers \(K(L,n)\) recursively by
\[
 K(L,0)=0,\qquad
 K(L,n+1)=L+1+L K(L,n). \tag{3}
\]
We will use the following branching observation.

Suppose that \(H\) is finite and that, for every set \(F\) of fewer than \(D\) edges, there are sets \(U_F\) of at most \(L+1\) vertices and \(E_F\) of at most \(L\) edges such that:

* \(E_F\cap F=\varnothing\);
* every binary coloring of \(H[U_F]\) makes at least one edge of \(E_F\) monochromatic.

Then there is a set \(U\) of at most \(K(L,D)\) vertices such that
\[
 \beta(H[U])\geq D. \tag{4}
\]

Here is the full branching argument. More generally, starting with an already forbidden set \(F\), and with \(|F|+n\leq D\), we construct a set of at most \(K(L,n)\) vertices such that every binary coloring makes \(n\) distinct edges outside \(F\) monochromatic. For \(n=0\), take the empty set. For \(n+1\), use \(U_F,E_F\). For every \(e\in E_F\), recursively construct the depth-\(n\) set with forbidden set \(F\cup\{e\}\). Take the union of \(U_F\) and all these child sets. There are at most \(L\) children, so its size is at most
\[
 L+1+L K(L,n)=K(L,n+1).
\]
Given a coloring, choose a monochromatic \(e\in E_F\), then use the child belonging to \(e\), which supplies another \(n\) monochromatic edges disjoint from \(F\cup\{e\}\). This proves the induction and hence (4).

We now obtain the required small obstructions from odd closed walks. Suppose a graph \(Q\) has the property that any two vertices in the same component can be joined by a walk of length at most \(M\). If \(Q\) is not bipartite, it has an odd closed walk of length at most \(2M+1\). To see this directly, choose a root in each component and, for every vertex \(x\), choose a root-to-\(x\) walk of length at most \(M\). Color \(x\) by the parity of the chosen walk length. Since the graph is not bipartite, some edge \(xy\) has equally colored endpoints. Concatenating the root-to-\(x\) walk, the edge \(xy\), and the reverse of the root-to-\(y\) walk gives an odd closed walk of length at most \(2M+1\).

An odd closed walk \(P\) of length at most \(L\) supplies exactly the obstruction required above: use its support, of size at most \(L+1\), and the set of its edges, of size at most \(L\). Every binary coloring makes some edge of an odd closed walk monochromatic, since colors would otherwise alternate around the walk and could not return to the starting color after an odd number of steps.

We next bound component diameters from a radius cover. Suppose a finite graph \(Q\) has a set \(T\) of at most \(q\) centers and every vertex is joined to some center by a walk of length at most \(R\). Then any two vertices in the same component can be joined by a walk of length at most
\[
 q(2R+1)+2R. \tag{5}
\]
For completeness, assign to every vertex \(x\) a center \(r(x)\) and an \(x\)-to-\(r(x)\) walk of length at most \(R\). Whenever \(xy\) is an edge, the centers \(r(x),r(y)\) can be joined by a walk of length at most \(2R+1\). Form an auxiliary graph on the centers, joining two distinct centers whenever such a walk exists. A path in the original graph induces connectivity of the corresponding centers in this auxiliary graph. A simple path in an auxiliary graph on at most \(q\) vertices uses at most \(q\) edges. Replacing each auxiliary edge by its walk and adding the initial and terminal radius-\(R\) walks gives (5).

Define
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 M(q,R,D)&=(q+2D)(2R+1)+2R,\\
 L(q,R,D)&=2M(q,R,D)+1,\\
 \rho(q,R,D)&=K(L(q,R,D),D). \tag{6}
 \end{aligned}
\]

We claim:

**Bounded-radius kernel lemma.** If \(H\) is finite, \(\beta(H)\geq D\), and \(H\) has at most \(q\) centers such that every vertex is within walk distance \(R\) of a center, then there is \(U\subseteq V(H)\) with
\[
 |U|\leq \rho(q,R,D),\qquad \beta(H[U])\geq D. \tag{7}
\]

To prove this, fix any edge set \(F\) with \(|F|<D\). The graph \(H-F\) is not bipartite, for otherwise \(\beta(H)\leq |F|<D\). The original radius cover can be modified into one for \(H-F\): follow a chosen path from a vertex toward its center until just before the first deleted edge. If no deleted edge occurs, one reaches the old center; otherwise one reaches an endpoint of an edge in \(F\). Thus every vertex is within distance \(R\), in \(H-F\), of
\[
 T\cup \operatorname{Ends}(F).
\]
This set has at most \(q+2|F|\leq q+2D\) vertices. By (5), any reachable pair in \(H-F\) has a connecting walk of length at most \(M(q,R,D)\). Since \(H-F\) is nonbipartite, it therefore has an odd closed walk of length at most \(L(q,R,D)\). Its edges avoid \(F\), and its support and edge set give the obstruction needed for the branching argument. Applying that argument gives (7).

--------------------------------------------------------------------
2. Weighted heights rooted at the bad edges
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Let \(G\) be finite and let \(c:V(G)\to\{0,1\}\) be a binary coloring. Call an edge bad if its endpoints have the same \(c\)-color, and good otherwise. Let \(B\) be the spanning graph consisting only of the good edges. Let \(S\) be a set containing an endpoint of every bad edge; later, \(S\) will be the set of all such endpoints.

Fix a radius parameter \(R\). Define a weighted height \(h(v)\) as follows. Among all good-edge walks from some \(s\in S\) to \(v\), minimize
\[
 \operatorname{length}(P)+c(s), \tag{8}
\]
where \(c(s)\) is regarded as either 0 or 1. If no such walk exists, set
\[
 h(v)=2(R+2)+c(v). \tag{9}
\]
The deliberately large value in (9) places unreachable vertices above the radius under consideration while preserving parity.

These heights have four important properties.

First,
\[
 h(s)\leq1\quad(s\in S), \tag{10}
\]
using the length-zero walk.

Second,
\[
 h(v)\equiv c(v)\pmod 2. \tag{11}
\]
Indeed, colors alternate along every good edge, so for a good walk from \(s\) to \(v\), its length plus \(c(s)\) has parity \(c(v)\). Formula (9) has the same parity when no such walk exists.

Third, for every edge \(xy\) of \(G\),
\[
 h(x)\leq h(y)+1,
 \qquad h(y)\leq h(x)+1. \tag{12}
\]
For a good edge this follows by extending a minimizing walk by that edge; if one endpoint is unreachable, so is the other. For a bad edge, both endpoints lie in \(S\), so both heights are at most 1, which also gives (12).

Fourth, if \(xy\) is an edge and \(h(y)>1\), then \(xy\) cannot be bad, because a bad edge would put \(y\) in \(S\) and hence give \(h(y)\leq1\). Thus \(xy\) is good. Combining (11) and (12), the two heights have opposite parity and differ by at most one, so
\[
 h(x)+1=h(y)\quad\hbox{or}\quad h(y)+1=h(x). \tag{13}
\]

There is also a localized form of the bounded-radius lemma. Let
\[
 A_R=\{v:h(v)\leq R\}.
\]
Every \(v\in A_R\) has a minimizing good walk from \(S\) of length at most \(R\), and every vertex on its initial segments also has height at most \(R\). Hence, inside \(G[A_R]\), every vertex is within distance \(R\) of \(S\cap A_R\). Consequently, if \(|S|\leq q\) and
\[
 \beta(G[A_R])\geq D,
\]
then the bounded-radius kernel lemma gives a set \(U\subseteq A_R\) such that
\[
 |U|\leq\rho(q,R,D),\qquad \beta(G[U])\geq D. \tag{14}
\]

--------------------------------------------------------------------
3. Compressing a plateau between two height balls
--------------------------------------------------------------------

We next prove the plateau-compression construction that handles the case where (14) cannot extract the full distance.

Suppose \(h:V(G)\to\mathbb N\) satisfies (12) and (13). Let
\[
 1\leq a<t,\qquad t+3\leq b,

a nd suppose
\[
 \beta(G[\{h\leq a\}])=\beta(G[\{h\leq b\}]). \tag{15}
\]
Assume also that \(G\) is not 3-colorable.

Choose an optimal binary coloring \(k\) of the outer graph \(G[\{h\leq b\}]\). Its bad edges all lie in the inner graph \(G[\{h\leq a\}]\). Here is why. The set of bad edges in the inner graph is a subset of the set of bad edges in the outer graph. The latter has cardinality equal to the common value in (15). The former has cardinality at least the minimum \(\beta(G[\{h\leq a\}])\), which is the same number. Therefore these two bad-edge sets are equal. In particular,
\[
 xy\in E(G),\ h(x),h(y)\leq b,\ k(x)=k(y)
 \quad\Longrightarrow\quad h(x),h(y)\leq a. \tag{16}
\]

For \(x\in V(G)\), define a boundary label
\[
 \lambda(x)=k(x)+h(x)+t\pmod 2. \tag{17}
\]
Construct a new graph \(J\) with vertex set
\[
 V(G)\sqcup\{p_0,p_1\}.
\]
Its old-old edges are exactly the edges \(xy\) of \(G\) with \(h(x),h(y)\leq t\). In addition, if \(h(x)=t\), join \(x\) to the apex \(p_{\lambda(x)}\). There are no edges between the two apex vertices.

We establish three properties of \(J\).

**(i) \(J\) is not 3-colorable.** Suppose instead that \(J\) has a proper coloring \(\gamma\) with colors \(0,1,2\). We extend it to all of \(G\). For \(h(x)\leq t\), retain \(\gamma(x)\). For \(h(x)=t+1\), give \(x\) the color \(\gamma(p_{\lambda(x)})\). For \(h(x)=t+2\), choose a color different from both \(\gamma(p_{\lambda(x)})\) and 0; this is always possible with three colors. For \(h(x)\geq t+3\), use color 0 or 1 according to the parity of \(h(x)\), with height \(t+3\) receiving color 0.

We verify that this is proper. An edge entirely below height \(t\) is handled by the coloring of \(J\). Across heights \(t,t+1\), the endpoint at height \(t\) is adjacent in \(J\) to the relevant apex. Across heights \(t+1,t+2\), the buffer color was chosen different from the apex color. Across heights \(t+2,t+3\), the buffer color is different from 0. Above this, colors alternate because adjacent heights differ exactly by one.

It remains only to check that adjacent vertices in the three-layer annulus use the same label whenever the rule requires it. In this annulus the heights exceed \(a\), so (16) says that \(k\) changes across every edge. By (13), height parity also changes across every edge. Therefore the two changes cancel in (17), and \(\lambda\) is constant across such an edge. Thus the extension is indeed a proper 3-coloring of \(G\), a contradiction.

**(ii) The total bipartization distance does not increase:**
\[
 \beta(J)\leq \beta(G[\{h\leq b\}]). \tag{18}
\]
Color every old vertex \(x\) by \(k(x)\), and color \(p_i\) by \(1-i\). At height \(t\), (17) gives
\[
 \lambda(x)=k(x)+2t\equiv k(x)\pmod2,
\]
so every old-apex edge is properly colored. Thus all bad edges of this coloring of \(J\) are old-old bad edges of \(k\), and these are among the bad edges in the outer ball. This proves (18).

**(iii) Small induced subgraphs of \(J\) inherit no larger distance from \(G\).** More precisely, for any \(X\subseteq V(J)\) with
\[
 |X|<t-a, \tag{19}
\]
let \(X_0=X\cap V(G)\). Then
\[
 \beta(J[X])\leq \beta(G[X_0]). \tag{20}
\]

There are \(t-a\) integer levels strictly above \(a\) and at most \(t\). By (19), some level \(m\), with \(a<m\leq t\), contains no old vertex of \(X\). Let \(d\) be an optimal binary coloring of \(G[X_0]\). Color old vertices of \(J[X]\) by \(d\) below level \(m\), and by \(k\) at or above level \(m\); color \(p_i\) by \(1-i\).

No edge of \(J[X]\) can cross this splice: by (12), adjacent heights differ by at most one, and crossing from below \(m\) to at least \(m\) would force an endpoint at the absent level \(m\). Below the splice, every bad edge is a bad edge for \(d\) in \(G[X_0]\). At or above the splice, a bad old-old edge would be a \(k\)-bad edge with a height greater than \(a\), contradicting (16). Old-apex edges are proper for the same boundary calculation used in (ii). Hence the number of bad edges is at most the optimum for \(G[X_0]\), proving (20).

Together, (i), (18), and (20) constitute the plateau-compression lemma.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
4. Uniform finite witnesses
--------------------------------------------------------------------

Define a rapidly growing sequence \(W(D)\) by
\[
 W(0)=0

a nd, for \(D\geq0\),
\[
 \begin{aligned}
 s_D&=2W(D)+8,\\
 R_D&=2+(D+1)s_D,\\
 W(D+1)&=W(D)+1+ho\bigl(2(D+1),R_D,D+1\bigr). \tag{21}
 \end{aligned}
\]
In particular, \(W\) is nondecreasing.

We prove the following uniform finite-witness theorem by induction on \(D\).

**Finite-witness theorem.** If \(G\) is a finite non-3-colorable graph and \(\beta(G)\leq D\), then there are an integer \(d\) and a vertex set \(X\) such that
\[
 1\leq d\leq D,\qquad |X|\leq W(d),\qquad \beta(G[X])\geq d. \tag{22}
\]

For \(D=0\), there is no such \(G\): \(\beta(G)=0\) makes \(G\) bipartite, hence 3-colorable.

Assume the result through \(D\), and let \(G\) be non-3-colorable with \(\beta(G)\leq D+1\). If \(\beta(G)\leq D\), apply the induction hypothesis. We may therefore assume
\[
 \beta(G)=D+1. \tag{23}
\]
Choose an optimal binary coloring \(c\) of \(G\), and let \(S\) be the set of endpoints of its bad edges. There are \(D+1\) bad edges, so
\[
 |S|\leq2(D+1). \tag{24}
\]
Use the good-edge graph, the root set \(S\), and radius
\[
 R=R_D=2+(D+1)(2W(D)+8)

to construct the weighted height \(h\) of Section 2.

There are now two cases.

**Case 1: the radius-\(R\) ball retains full distance.** If
\[
 \beta(G[\{h\leq R\}])\geq D+1,
\]
then (14), with \(q=2(D+1)\), supplies \(X\) with
\[
 |X|\leq \rho(2(D+1),R,D+1)\leq W(D+1)

a nd \(\beta(G[X])\geq D+1\). Thus (22) holds with \(d=D+1\).

**Case 2: the radius-\(R\) ball has smaller distance.** Put
\[
 s=2W(D)+8

a nd define, for \(0\leq j\leq D+1\),
\[
 m(j)=\beta\bigl(G[\{h\leq 2+js\}]\bigr). \tag{25}
\]
The function \(m(j)\) is nondecreasing, because the balls are nested. Moreover,
\[
 m(D+1)<D+1, \tag{26}
\]
because \(2+(D+1)s=R\) and we are in Case 2.

There must be some \(j<D+1\) with
\[
 m(j)=m(j+1). \tag{27}
\]
Indeed, if every one of the first \(D+1\) steps were a strict increase, then, since the values are nonnegative integers, induction would give \(m(D+1)\geq D+1\), contradicting (26).

Set
\[
 a=2+js,
 \qquad b=2+(j+1)s,
 \qquad t=a+2W(D)+4. \tag{28}
\]
Then \(a<t\), \(a\geq1\), and
\[
 t+3\leq b,
\]
because \(b-a=s=2W(D)+8\). The height properties (12) and (13), together with the plateau (27), allow us to apply the construction of Section 3. We obtain a finite graph \(J\) such that

* \(J\) is not 3-colorable;
* \(\beta(J)\leq m(j+1)\leq m(D+1)\leq D\), where the last inequality follows from (26);
* whenever \(Y\subseteq V(J)\) has \(|Y|<t-a\), and \(Y_0=Y\cap V(G)\),
\[
 \beta(J[Y])\leq\beta(G[Y_0]). \tag{29}
\]

Apply the induction hypothesis to \(J\). It gives \(1\leq d\leq D\) and \(Y\subseteq V(J)\) such that
\[
 |Y|\leq W(d),\qquad \beta(J[Y])\geq d. \tag{30}
\]
Since \(W\) is nondecreasing,
\[
 |Y|\leq W(D)<2W(D)+4=t-a.
\]
Thus (29) applies. For \(X=Y\cap V(G)\),
\[
 |X|\leq |Y|\leq W(d)

a nd
\[
 \beta(G[X])\geq\beta(J[Y])\geq d.
\]
This proves (22) and completes the induction.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
5. Diagonal choice of the divergent function
--------------------------------------------------------------------

We now choose a function that grows too slowly to permit any of the finite witnesses above.

For \(i\geq0\), put
\[
 N_i=W(i+1).
\]
Define
\[
 f(n)=\min\Bigl(\{n\}\cup\{i:n\leq N_i\}\Bigr). \tag{31}
\]
The set is nonempty because it contains \(n\).

The function \(f\) is nondecreasing. If \(n\leq m\), then every index satisfying \(m\leq N_i\) also satisfies \(n\leq N_i\), while the fallback candidate rises from \(n\) to \(m\). More explicitly, any candidate in the set defining \(f(m)\) bounds \(f(n)\) from above: the candidate \(m\) is at least \(n\geq f(n)\), and an index \(i\) eligible at \(m\) is also eligible at \(n\), so \(f(n)\leq i\). Hence \(f(n)\leq f(m)\).

Also,
\[
 f(W(d))<d\qquad(d\geq1), \tag{32}
\]
because in (31), for \(n=W(d)=N_{d-1}\), the index \(d-1\) is an eligible candidate.

Finally, \(f(n)\to\infty\). Fix \(k\). Choose \(I>k\), and let
\[
 B=\max\{N_i:i<I\},

taking \(B=0\) if necessary. If \(n>\max(B,k)\), then the fallback candidate \(n\) is greater than \(k\), while no index \(i<I\) is eligible, because \(n>B\geq N_i\). Every eligible index is therefore at least \(I>k\). Thus \(f(n)>k\) for all sufficiently large \(n\), proving divergence.

--------------------------------------------------------------------
6. The chosen profile forces 3-colorability
--------------------------------------------------------------------

First let \(G\) be finite and suppose that for every \(n\),
\[
 G.\operatorname{maxSubgraphEdgeDistToBipartite}(n)\leq f(n). \tag{33}
\]
We claim that \(G\) is 3-colorable. If not, apply the finite-witness theorem with \(D=\beta(G)\). We obtain \(d\geq1\) and \(X\subseteq V(G)\) such that
\[
 |X|\leq W(d),\qquad \beta(G[X])\geq d.
\]
On the other hand, (2) and (33) give
\[
 \beta(G[X])\leq f(|X|).
\]
Since \(f\) is nondecreasing,
\[
 d\leq \beta(G[X])\leq f(|X|)
 \leq f(W(d))<d,
\]
a contradiction. Therefore every finite graph satisfying (33) is 3-colorable.

Now let \(G\) be an arbitrary, possibly infinite, graph satisfying (33). Every finite induced subgraph \(G[X]\) also satisfies the same profile bound. Indeed, any finite subgraph of \(G[X]\) embeds injectively into \(G\), and pulling back deleted edges or binary colorings shows that its bipartization distance is no greater than the corresponding distance in \(G\). Taking maxima gives
\[
 (G[X]).\operatorname{maxSubgraphEdgeDistToBipartite}(n)
 \leq G.\operatorname{maxSubgraphEdgeDistToBipartite}(n)
 \leq f(n).
\]
Hence every finite induced subgraph of \(G\) is 3-colorable.

By the standard compactness theorem for finite graph coloring, \(G\) itself is 3-colorable. One direct proof is to consider the compact product space \(\{0,1,2\}^{V(G)}\). For every edge \(xy\), the condition that the colors at \(x\) and \(y\) differ is closed. Every finite collection of these conditions involves only finitely many vertices and is satisfiable because the corresponding finite induced subgraph is 3-colorable. The finite-intersection property and compactness therefore give a coloring satisfying all edge conditions simultaneously.

We have thus constructed a nondecreasing function \(f:\mathbb N\to\mathbb N\) with \(f(n)\to\infty\) such that every graph satisfying the proposed local bipartization bound is 3-colorable. In particular, every such graph has chromatic number at most 3, not infinite. Applying the conjectured assertion to this particular divergent \(f\) would produce a graph which simultaneously has infinite chromatic number and is 3-colorable, an impossibility. Therefore the formalized conjecture is false.
